title: Best Moisture Absorber Dehumidifiers (2026): DampRid vs. Eva-Dry
h1: The Best Moisture Absorber Dehumidifiers for Closets, Safes and Storage
dek: No plug, no noise, no fuss: the right tub, bag or canister keeps a small, closed space dry for pennies a week.
description: The best moisture absorber dehumidifiers for closets, pantries, gun safes and storage units, from refillable DampRid tubs to rechargeable Eva-Dry silica.
intro: A moisture absorber is the simplest dehumidifier there is: a tub, bag or canister of desiccant that sits quietly in a corner and pulls water vapor out of the air with no cord and no motor. Most moisture absorber dehumidifiers are filled with **calcium chloride** crystals that slowly turn into a salty liquid as they work. The rest use **silica gel** beads that trap water inside and can be dried out and used again.

Both kinds do a genuinely useful job — but only in the right place. In a closed closet, cabinet, safe or parked RV, a few ounces of crystals can keep up with the small amount of moisture in the air. In an open basement that wicks water through concrete all day, they simply can't. We sorted the main US options by maker-rated coverage, how long each one lasts, how it holds the water it collects and what it costs to keep going, so you can match the product to the space.
topPicksLead: For most closets, bathrooms and pantries, the **DampRid Refillable Moisture Absorber** is the one to buy: it's rated for up to 250 square feet, and cheap refill bags make it the lowest-cost way to stay dry all year.

products.name: DampRid Refillable Moisture Absorber (10.5 oz)
pros: Rated for spaces up to 250 sq ft
Bulk refill bags keep running costs tiny
Clear tub shows exactly how much water it has pulled
cons: Brine has to be poured out by hand
products.whyWeLoveIt: This is the most economical way to keep a small room or closet dry month after month. You buy the tub once, then top it up from a refill bag, and the collected water sits in plain view so you always know it's working. DampRid says the fragrance-free version is safe to use around food, which makes it our choice for a pantry.
products.performance: DampRid rates each 10.5-ounce fill for up to 45 days in up to 250 square feet, with the caveat that hot, humid weather uses it up faster. Its 42-ounce refill bag fills the tub four times, and a larger 7.5-pound Super Refill covers about 11 fills. When the crystals are fully dissolved, you pour the brine into a toilet — DampRid says it's septic safe — and refill. The maker also notes the crystals will clump into a hard mass before they dissolve; that's normal, and you shouldn't break it up or add fresh crystals early.
products.notes: Set it on a flat shelf rather than the floor, where a pet or vacuum can tip it.

products.name: DampRid Hanging Moisture Absorber (15.4 oz)

products.whyWeLoveIt: Most reach-in closets have spare rod space and nothing else, and that's exactly where this bag lives. It hangs between your clothes, collects water in a see-through pocket at the bottom and goes in the trash in one piece when it's full.
products.performance: DampRid rates the 15.4-ounce bag for up to 60 days, and it's sold in single bags and multipacks — the packs are usually the better buy. The maker is clear that you shouldn't cut the bag open: when the liquid reaches the fill line, toss it whole. It also asks for some air space around the bag, so don't sandwich it between heavy winter coats. If a closet that shares a wall with a shower stays damp after a month, step up to one of our [closet dehumidifier picks](/best/best-dehumidifier-for-closet/).

products.whyWeLoveIt: A storage unit, a winterized cabin or a boat on stands rarely has an outlet, and nobody wants to visit every few weeks. One big tub can ride out a whole off-season in a modest space with no attention at all.

When the dark liquid layer reaches the red arrow, the whole tub goes in the trash. Check the weight on the label before you buy: some stores now carry a roughly 3-pound bucket with similar branding and noticeably fewer crystals. For a powered option, see our [storage unit dehumidifier guide](/best/best-dehumidifier-for-storage-unit/).

products.whyWeLoveIt: Calcium chloride turns into salt water, and salt water is the last thing you want near a rifle, a camera or a circuit board. The E-333 holds its moisture inside sealed silica beads, so there's nothing to spill — which is why it's also our top pick for [gun safes](/best/best-dehumidifier-for-gun-safe/).
products.performance: Eva-Dry rates it for up to 333 cubic feet and up to 13 ounces of water per charge, and says it has sold more than 3 million. The beads shift from orange to green when they're saturated; you then plug the whole canister into a wall outlet for 10 to 12 hours to dry it out. Retail listings put it at roughly 20 to 30 days between recharges, depending on how damp the space is.
products.notes: It's also a good fit for a car you drive daily, where a spilled tub of brine would be a mess.

Eva-Dry lists closets, safes, RVs, boats and seasonal storage among its intended uses.

items.label: Water a DampRid tub removed from open air in CHOICE's 65%-humidity test
Humidity drop in CHOICE's sealed, closet-sized chamber over three days
The EPA's recommended indoor humidity range, with 60% as the ceiling

blocks.text: Those first two numbers tell the whole story. Australia's consumer group CHOICE found that in an open room, a DampRid tub pulls out only about 2 milliliters of water an hour — while the electric dehumidifiers in its review removed somewhere between 113 and 388. Yet in a sealed, closet-sized box, the same tub dragged humidity from 80% down to 43% in three days and collected almost half a cup of water. Small and closed is where absorbers shine.

We don't run a lab. Instead, we start from what manufacturers publish and stand behind: rated coverage and lifespan from product pages, active-ingredient percentages from safety data sheets, and disposal and placement instructions from each maker's FAQ. We add independent measurements where they exist — chiefly CHOICE's published DampRid results — and the EPA's humidity guidance.

From there we weighed how each product holds the water it collects (brine or sealed beads), how long it lasts per fill or charge, whether you can refill or reuse it, and how much it costs to keep running over a year. We also read owner reviews for recurring complaints like leaking tubs and hardened crystals.

sections.heading: What to look for in a moisture absorber

items.label: The right format for the space
items.text: A hanging bag for a clothes closet, a refillable tub for a bathroom or pantry, a big tub for a storage unit, and a silica canister for anything sealed.

items.label: Refillable if it's permanent
items.text: If the absorber will live in the same spot all year, a refillable tub plus bulk crystals costs a fraction of buying new disposables every couple of months.

items.label: Silica near metal and electronics
items.text: Calcium chloride brine is salt water. Keep it away from tools, firearms, cameras and anything with a circuit board.

items.label: A stable spot
items.text: DampRid describes its tubs as spill-resistant, not spill-proof. A flat shelf beats the floor every time.

items.label: A cheap hygrometer
items.text: A digital humidity gauge tells you whether the space is actually above 60% and whether the absorber is bringing it down. Our [placement guide](/guides/where-to-place-a-dehumidifier/) covers where to put both.

head: Calcium chloride (DampRid, Arm & Hammer)
Silica gel (Eva-Dry)
rows: Crystals dissolve into brine in the tub or bag
Closets, pantries, storage units, stored vehicles

blocks.text: Calcium chloride absorbs more water for the money and keeps going until it has fully dissolved. Silica holds less per cycle, so it belongs in a sealed safe or cabinet rather than a damp room — but it can never leak salt water onto something you care about.

blocks.title: Same company, different label
blocks.text: Arm & Hammer's moisture absorbers are made under license by W.M. Barr — the company behind DampRid. Its safety data sheet lists 65–85% calcium chloride versus 80–100% for DampRid, and the small tubs cost noticeably more per ounce than DampRid refill crystals. Buy it for the scent if you like, not the value.

items: **Charcoal and bamboo charcoal bags.** They're odor absorbers. DampRid's own FAQ says its charcoal-based product tackles smells but doesn't remove excess moisture.
**Open boxes of baking soda.** Great in the fridge, useless as a desiccant.
**Bowls of rice.** In a widely reported months-long weighing comparison, silica gel absorbed far more water than rice — and rice wasn't even the runner-up.

sections.heading: Moisture absorber vs. dehumidifier: when you need a machine

blocks.text: A closed closet only holds a few ounces of water vapor at any one time, so an absorber's slow trickle is plenty. A basement is a different animal: moisture keeps arriving through the slab, the walls and the outside air, and no tub can keep pace. If a space still smells musty after a month of absorbers, or a hygrometer reads above 60% for weeks, it's time for a machine — start with our [basement dehumidifier picks](/best/best-dehumidifier-for-basement/) or, for a single room, our [best small dehumidifiers](/best/best-small-dehumidifier/).

items: Keep tubs and bags out of reach of kids and pets. DampRid's safety data sheet classes the crystals as a skin and serious eye irritant and harmful if swallowed.
Empty refillable tubs only after every crystal has dissolved, then pour the brine into a toilet or a running sink.
Never cut open a hanging bag — throw it away whole.

blocks.text: The **DampRid Refillable** tub is the best moisture absorber for most closets, bathrooms and pantries — rated for 250 square feet and about the cheapest way to stay dry year-round. Hang a **DampRid Hanging** bag in a clothes closet, park a **4-pound Hi-Capacity tub** in a storage unit or stored RV, and choose a rechargeable **Eva-Dry E-333** or **E-500** for safes, cabinets and anything metal. If the musty smell keeps coming back, you've outgrown absorbers; our [best dehumidifier guide](/best/best-dehumidifier/) is the next step.

faqs.q: What is the best moisture absorber?
faqs.a: For most closets and small rooms, the DampRid Refillable Moisture Absorber. DampRid rates the 10.5-ounce tub for up to 250 square feet and up to 45 days per fill, and bulk refill bags keep the running cost very low. For safes and electronics, choose a rechargeable silica unit like the Eva-Dry E-333.

faqs.q: Is a moisture absorber the same as a dehumidifier?
faqs.a: Not quite. A moisture absorber is a passive desiccant with no power, fan or compressor, so it only pulls a small amount of water from the air around it. An electric dehumidifier actively moves air across a cold coil or desiccant wheel and removes many times more. Absorbers suit closets, safes and cabinets; dehumidifiers suit rooms and basements.

Yes, in small, closed spaces. In CHOICE's sealed, closet-sized chamber, a DampRid tub dropped humidity from 80% to 43% in three days. In an open room the effect is tiny — about 2 milliliters of water an hour, against more than 100 for even modest electric dehumidifiers.

DampRid rates its hanging bag for up to 60 days, its 10.5-ounce tubs for up to 45 days in 250 square feet, and its 4-pound Hi-Capacity tub for up to six months in a small space. All of them run out faster in hot, humid weather.

faqs.q: Can I use a moisture absorber in a gun safe?
faqs.a: Use silica, not calcium chloride. Silica gel traps water inside the beads, so nothing can drip onto steel. The Eva-Dry E-333 is rated for 333 cubic feet — enough for most safes — and recharges overnight from a wall outlet.
